Algebra and Logic, Vol. 48, No. 3, 2009




NORMAL RELATIVELY CONVEX
SUBGROUPS OF SOLVABLE
ORDERABLE GROUPS
     V. V. Bludov,1∗ V. M. Kopytov,2
     and A. H. Rhemtulla3                                                                      UDC 512.54


                                                                         To the memory of N. Ya. Medvedev
    Keywords: ordered group, solvable group, convex subgroup.

      Orderable solvable groups in which every relatively convex subgroup is normal are studied. If
      such a class is subgroup closed than it is precisely the class of solvable orderable groups which
      are locally of ﬁnite (Mal’tsev) rank. A criterion for an orderable metabelian group to have every
      relatively convex subgroup normal is given. Examples of an orderable solvable group G of length
      three with periodic G/G and of an orderable solvable group of length four with only one proper
      normal relatively convex subgroup are constructed.


                                               INTRODUCTION

    It is well known that every convex subgroup of an ordered locally nilpotent group is normal, and this
is also true of ordered Engel groups; but this property does not extend to ordered solvable groups. It was
shown in [1, Cor. 5.3.1] that every non-Abelian solvable ordered group has at least one proper (nontrivial)
normal convex subgroup, and this is about the best that one can say in general.
    In this paper, we study orderable solvable groups in which every relatively convex subgroup is normal.
We show that if such a class is subgroup closed, then it coincides with the class of solvable orderable groups
which are locally of ﬁnite (Mal’tsev) rank. This result is presented in Sec. 2. A criterion for an orderable
metabelian group to have every relatively convex subgroup normal is given in Sec. 3. This is followed by
examples of metabelian orderable groups having nonnormal convex subgroups for every order on the group.
An example of a solvable orderable group G such that G/G is periodic is taken up in Sec. 4, thus answering
[2, Question 5.25]. A minor generalization of that example enables us to construct an orderable solvable
group of length four with only one proper normal relatively convex subgroup (Example 3.4).
    We give the notation and deﬁnitions. The sets of natural, integer, rational, and real numbers are denoted
by N, Z, Q, and R, respectively. We write γn (G) = [G, . . . , G] for the nth term of the lower central series

in G and write H  G for the restricted wreath product of groups H and G. A cyclic group of order p and

   A subgroup H is isolated (strictly isolated) in a group G if g n ∈ H (g 1+f1 +...+fn ∈ H) implies g ∈ H for
any g, f1 , . . . , fn ∈ G, n ⩾ 1. If H is a subgroup of G then I(H) denotes the isolator of H in G (i.e., the
minimal isolated subgroup of G which contains H). We call G an R∗ -group if {1} is strictly isolated in G.
    Deﬁnition 1. An N-group is an orderable group in which every relatively convex subgroup is normal.
An Ns -group is one in which every subgroup is an N-group. By N and Ns we denote the classes of N- and
Ns -groups, respectively.
    Let S(a) denote the semigroup generated by all conjugates of a in G.
      Deﬁnition 2 [3]. We call G an R+ -group if aG /bG  is periodic for every b ∈ S(a).


                                               1. Ns -GROUPS

   It is well known that a wreath product a  t of two inﬁnite cyclic groups has nonnormal relatively
convex subgroups (see [4; 5, Sec. 2.1]), and so a  t is not an N-group. Therefore, an Ns -group does not
contain a subgroup isomorphic to a  t. We also observe that a wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic
groups a and t admits orders with both inﬁnitely and ﬁnitely many normal convex subgroups. The
inﬁnite case is realized when a series of all convex subgroups is precisely a lower central series of a group.
The ﬁnite case arises when we ﬁx a positive integer n, require that γi (a  t) are convex for i = 1, . . . , n,
and then deﬁne the lexicographic order on γn (a  t).
      THEOREM A. A ﬁnitely generated solvable Ns -group has ﬁnite (Mal’tsev) rank.
   LEMMA 1.1. Let G be a solvable orderable group that is locally of ﬁnite rank. Then every relatively
convex subgroup is normal in G and every isolated normal subgroup of G is relatively convex.
   Proof. If G has ﬁnite rank then every relatively convex subgroup of G is normal in G [4, Chap. II,
Sec. 2, Prop. 5]. Suppose that G is locally of ﬁnite rank and let C be a relatively convex subgroup of G.
Then C ∩ L is normal in L for every ﬁnitely generated subgroup L. If we take L to be the subgroup c, g
we see that cg ∈ C for every c ∈ C and every g ∈ G. Hence, C is normal in G.
   Now let N be an isolated normal subgroup of G and suppose that G/N is not orderable. Then there is
a ﬁnitely generated subgroup L of G such that LN/N is not orderable. Therefore, N ∩ L is not relatively
convex in L. But every isolated normal subgroup of a ﬁnitely generated orderable solvable group of ﬁnite
rank is relatively convex [5, Thm. 4.1.1]. Contradiction. 2
    LEMMA 1.2. Suppose that G is a ﬁnitely generated solvable Ns -group such that G does not have
ﬁnite rank but G is locally of ﬁnite rank. Put J = I(G ). Then:
    (1) J is locally nilpotent;
    (2) the solvability length of J is n − 1, where n is the solvability length of G;
    (3) there exist t ∈ G \ J and a ∈ J such that H = a, t has a quotient H/K that is isomorphic to
Cp  C∞ , with Ka the base group and Kt the top group.
    Proof. (1) Let L be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of G and ≤ be an order on G. Let C be the union
of all convex subgroups Xi of G such that Xi ∩ L < L. Then C ∩ L < L since L is ﬁnitely generated. Let D
be the intersection of all convex subgroups that contain L. Then C ≺ D is a jump and [D, G ] ≤ C because
G centralizes all convex jumps. Since L ⊆ G , [L, D] ≤ C, it follows that L ≤ L1 , where L1 = C ∩ L. We
observe that L1 is the normal closure in L of a ﬁnitely generated subgroup and that it is isolated in L.



164
    Now let C1 ≺ D1 be a jump, where C1 is the union of all convex subgroups Xi of G satisfying Xi ∩ L1 <
L1 , and D1 is the intersection of all convex subgroups of G that contain L1 . Then [L, D1 ] ≤ C1 , and hence
[L, L1 ] ≤ L2 , where L2 = L1 ∩ C1 . Note that L2 is the normal closure in L of a ﬁnitely generated subgroup.
    The process is repeated until we obtain a descending chain Li of isolated subgroups of L. Since L has
ﬁnite rank, Lk = 1 for some ﬁnite integer k, and hence L is nilpotent.
    This shows that G is locally nilpotent. Since J/G is a periodic Abelian group, J is a locally nilpotent-
by-ﬁnite orderable group, and so it is locally nilpotent.
    (2) We use induction on the solvability length m of G . If G is Abelian, then so is J, since J/G is periodic
and J is orderable. If m > 1, then we let A be a maximal normal Abelian subgroup of J containing the
last nontrivial term of the derived series in G . Then A is isolated in J and J/A is orderable by Lemma 1.1.
The result now follows by induction since AG /A is solvable of length m − 1.
    (3) By [6], there are subgroups K < H ≤ G such that K is normal in H and H/K is isomorphic to Cp C∞
for some prime p. Thus, we can take H to be the subgroup a, t, in which case H/K = KaKt ∼       = Cp C∞ .
Now H is not contained in J for H is not nilpotent. More speciﬁcally, t ∈ J since its normal closure in
H contains a subgroup H1 = [a, t], t which has a quotient isomorphic to H/K. Replacing H with H1 if
necessary, we may assume that a ∈ J. This completes the proof of item (3). 2
   LEMMA 1.3. Let H = a, t be a torsion-free metabelian subgroup of G with the following properties:
   (1) G has an isolated normal Abelian subgroup J such that G/J is Abelian;
   (2) there are elements t ∈ G \ J and a ∈ J such that H = a, t, and for some normal subgroup K of
H, H/K = Ka  Kt ∼ = Cp  C∞ .
   Then H ∼ = C∞  C∞ .
   Proof. Note that K ⊆ B = at . Moreover, B is a direct product of cyclic groups Ai = at  for

    LEMMA 1.4. A ﬁnitely generated metabelian Ns -group has ﬁnite (Mal’tsev) rank.
    Proof. We use the notation established in Lemma 1.2. The group J is Abelian since G is metabelian.
By Lemma 1.2(3), there are t ∈ G \ J and a ∈ J such that H = a, t and H/K = Ka  Kt. Let
B = at . Then B is a direct product of inﬁnite cyclic groups Ai = at , and as shown in Lemma 1.3,

H = a  t ∼
              = C∞  C∞ . Since a wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic groups is not an N-group, G ∈ Ns . 2
    Proof of Theorem A. We use induction on the solvability length n of G. The case n = 2 was treated in
Lemma 1.4. Further, we adhere to the notation created in Lemma 1.2. By induction, we may assume that
G , and hence (by Lemma 1.2(2)) J, will be locally of ﬁnite rank. By Lemma 1.2(1), J is locally nilpotent.
Hence, J is solvable of length n − 1. Let Ji be the isolator of the (n − 1 − i)th derived subgroup of J. Then
1 = J0  J1  . . .  J(n−1) = J is a torsion-free Abelian series and each Ji is normal in G.
    If the rank of G is inﬁnite, then it follows by [6] that G contains a 2-generator subgroup H = a, t
having a quotient H/K = Ka  Kt ∼      = Cp  C∞ . Let i be the least integer such that G has such a section
with a ∈ Ji . If i = 1, then H is metabelian, and H ∈ N by Lemma 1.4, a contradiction. We assume i > 1.
    Every nontrivial normal subgroup of H/K contained in Kat /K is an inﬁnite direct product of cyclic
groups of order p, and Ji−1 , t is locally of ﬁnite rank by the choice of i. Hence, B ∩ Ji−1 ≤ K, where
B = at . Since H ∩ Ji−1 is locally nilpotent and the locally nilpotent radical of H/K is BK/K, it follows
that H ∩ Ji−1 ⊆ K(B ∩ Ji−1 ) ⊆ K. Thus, H/K is a quotient of H/H ∩ Ji−1 . Since a ∈ Ji , B ⊆ Ji .
Moreover, H/B is inﬁnite cyclic. Hence, H/(H ∩ Ji−1 ) is a torsion-free metabelian group with isolated
normal Abelian subgroup B/(H ∩ Ji−1 ).


                                                                                                              165
    Let H be a ﬁnitely generated subgroup of an Ns -group G. Then H too is an Ns -group. Now we apply
Lemma 1.3, with H/(H ∩ Ji−1 ) replacing H and B/(H ∩ Ji−1 ) replacing J in the statement of that lemma.
It follows that H/(H ∩ Ji−1 ) is isomorphic to a wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic groups. Such a group
is orderable, and so therefore are H and H/(H ∩ Ji−1 ). Hence, (H ∩ Ji−1 ) is a relatively convex subgroup of
H. But a wreath product of two inﬁnite cyclic groups is not an N-group. Thus, there is an order on H with
respect to which (H ∩ Ji−1 ) is convex, and there are other nonnormal convex subgroups of H containing
(H ∩ Ji−1 ). This shows that H ∈ N, a contradiction. 2
     PROPOSITION 1.5. If G is a solvable orderable group and all normal isolated subgroups of G are
relatively convex then G is an R+ -group.
     Proof. Let 1 = a ∈ G, b ∈ S(a), N (a) = aG , and N (b) = bG . We prove the proposition by
induction on the derived length of N (b). If N (b) is Abelian then its isolator I(N (b)) is Abelian and
I(N (b)) = {g ∈ G | g n ∈ N (b) for some positive n} (which is true for all nilpotent subgroups of orderable
groups; see [5, Lemma 2.6.6]). In this case I(N (b))/N (b) is periodic. By assumption, I(N (b)) is relatively
convex and, hence, is strictly isolated. This gives N (a) ≤ I(N (b)), and so N (a)/N (b) is periodic as well.
     Now we may assume that N (b) is solvable of length n > 1. Let A = (N (b))(n−1) so that A is a normal
Abelian subgroup of G and N (b)/A is solvable of length n − 1. The isolator I(A) is Abelian and is relatively
convex in G. Consider an orderable group Ḡ = G/I(A). If H̄ is a normal isolated subgroup of Ḡ, then I(A)H
is isolated in G; so I(A)H is a normal isolated subgroup of G, and by assumption, I(A)H is relatively convex
in G. Hence, H̄ is relatively convex in Ḡ and Ḡ satisﬁes the hypothesis of the proposition. By induction,
N̄ (a)/N̄ (b) is periodic, and so for every g ∈ N (a), there exist a positive n and elements d ∈ I(A) and
h ∈ N (b) such that g n = hd. Since A is Abelian, there exists a positive m for which d1 = dm ∈ A < N (b).
Hence, g nm = h1 d1 ∈ N (b) (here h1 is a product of conjugates of h, and so it belongs to N (b)). Thus,
N (a)/N (b) is periodic. 2


                  2. ORDERS UNDER WHICH ALL CONVEX SUBGROUPS
                                  ARE NORMAL

    Every non-Abelian solvable ordered group has at least one proper (nontrivial) normal convex subgroup
(see [1, Cor. 5.3.1]). In this section, we study the situation where all relatively convex subgroups are normal.
    THEOREM B. Let G be an orderable metabelian group. If rank(G/G ) = 1 then G admits a total
order under which all convex subgroups are normal. If, in addition, G is ﬁnitely generated then G has a
ﬁnite series of convex normal subgroups with Archimedean jumps.
    Proof. Let A be an isolator of G . It is known that A is Abelian, and it follows from the assumption
of the theorem that G/A is torsion-free Abelian of rank 1. Therefore, G/A is isomorphic to an additive
subgroup of rationals, and we can denote G/A by T = tr | r ∈ B, where B is a suitable subgroup of
rationals. If g1 , g2 ∈ G \ A have equal images in G/A, then ag1 = ag2 for all a ∈ A. Moreover, g ∩ A = {1}
for all g ∈ G \ A because G/A is torsion-free. Without loss of generality, we may replace G with a split
product A  T . Then we embed A into a divisible completion A∗ , extend actions of T to A∗ , and consider a
split product A∗  T . Thus, let G = A  T be an orderable metabelian group (i.e., a metabelian R∗ -group),
A be a divisible Abelian normal subgroup of G, and T be a torsion-free Abelian group of rank 1 written in
the form T = tr | r ∈ B ≤ Q.
    Choose an element a ∈ A. Let H(a) = SI(aG ) ≤ A be a strictly isolated normal subgroup generated
by a. The group H(a) is relatively convex because G/H(a) is a metabelian R∗ -group. Now we establish

a total order on G under which H(a) is convex and is ordered with an Archimedean order. Since H(a) is
relatively convex, we can ﬁnd a total order on G under which H(a) is convex, and if this order induces a
non-Archimedean order on H(a), then a and at are not Archimedean equivalent, i.e., a         at or a      at .

transﬁnite induction, we deﬁne on G a total order with a well-ordered series of convex subgroups of the
form H({aα }α<β ) or H({aα }α≤β ) and with the last subgroup A. All such groups are normal in G.
    If G is a ﬁnitely generated, then G satisﬁes the maximal condition for normal subgroups, so any well-
ordered ascendant chain of normal subgroups is ﬁnite, and hence we obtain an order on G with a ﬁnite
series of normal convex subgroups with Archimedean jumps. 2
    PROPOSITION 2.1. For every n > 1, there exist orderable metabelian groups Gn with n generators
having nonnormal convex subgroups for any ordering of Gn .
    Proof. It suﬃces to construct a 2-generator group with the required properties. Let M = M (x, y) be a
free metabelian group with free generators x and y. We put c = [x, y] and denote by N a normal subgroup

in M generated by cx+(y−1) , i.e., N = cx+(y−1) M . Let G = M/N .
    To show that G is orderable, it is enough to verify that G is an R∗ -group. Let h ∈ G so that

all coeﬃcients of g2 (x, y) are positive, and hence m0 + m1 + . . . + mk ⩾ 1.
    Taking y = 1 + ε in a small neighborhood of 1 and putting x = −(y − 1)2 = −ε2 , we obtain (x + (y −

1) ) = 0. On the other hand, g2 (x, y) belongs to a small neighborhood of g2,0 (y) which belongs to a small
neighborhood of m0 + m1 + . . . + mk ; so g2 (x, y) is not equal to zero, a contradiction. Thus, (x + (y − 1)2 )
divides g1 (x, y); hence h = 1 in G = M/N . Since h is arbitrary, G is an R∗ -group.
    Now we verify that G will contain a nonnormal convex subgroup once a total order has been established
on G. Let 1 = a ∈ G and H ≺ H  be a convex jump determined by a. If H is normal then G/H acts on
                                                                                          2
H  /H by multiplication by positive real numbers, and so H = (aH)x+(y−1) = (αx + (αy − 1)2 )aH = H, a
contradiction. 2
    We now point out solvable groups with ﬁnitely many relatively convex subgroups. Example 2.2 gives a
series of orderable metabelian groups with exactly n proper relatively convex subgroups for every positive
integer n. Of course, all relatively convex subgroups are normal in such groups.
   Example 2.2. Let V be a direct sum of n copies of additive groups of rationals. We think of V as
a vector space of dimension n over Q with basis e1 , . . . , en . Let t be a linear transformation of V deﬁned
thus:
                                    et1 .1 , eti .i + ei−1 , i = 2, . . . , n.                             (5)

Since t acts on V as a Jordan block, V contains exactly n + 1 invariant subspaces V0 = {0}, . . . , Vi =
e1 , . . . , ei , . . . , Vn = V . Let Gn be a split product of V and t where the action of t on V is given by
(5). Then Gn is an orderable metabelian group of ﬁnite rank, and hence all relatively convex subgroups of
Gn are normal. It easy to see that all subgroups Vi , i = 0, . . . , n, are relatively convex. Relations (5) yield
[e1 , t] = e1 , [ei , t] = ei + ei−1 , i = 2, . . . , n, and so ei t for all i. Consequently, V is an absolutely convex
subgroup. Moreover, all other relatively convex subgroups are contained in V because Gn /V has rank 1. If
H ≤ V is an isolated normal subgroup of Gn then H is an invariant subspace of V . Therefore, G has only
n proper relatively convex subgroups V1 , . . . , Vn . We also note that all Vi are absolutely convex.


                     3. AN ORDERED SOLVABLE GROUP WITH PERIODIC
                                 ABELIAN QUOTIENTS

    In [2, Question 5.25], it was conjectured that the quotient group G/G of a totally ordered solvable
group G is not periodic. Example 3.1 gives a negative answer to this question. A minor generalization of
this example allows us to construct an orderable solvable group of length four with only one proper normal
relatively convex subgroup (see Example 3.4).
    Example 3.1. We use an example of a right orderable group that is a generalization of Gorchakov’s
[7] (see also [4, Chap. I, Sec. 2, Example 9]).

   Let G be a group with generators cn , n ∈ Z, and relations

is metabelian. Relations (6) allow every (nontrivial) element g ∈ G to be represented as

    Now we deﬁne subgroups Ln = ci | i < n < G and Rn = ci | i ⩾ n < G, n ∈ Z. The deﬁning

following properties:
   LEMMA 3.2. For every integer n,
   (1) Ln is normal in G;
   (2) Ln+1 /Ln is inﬁnite cyclic;

    Now we construct a totally ordered group H as an extension of an Abelian group A by G. (Here we
employ the same approach as is used in Smirnov’s theorem [8]; see also [4, Chap. V, Sec. 4, Thm. 3 or
1, Thm. 3.5.1].) Smirnov’s construction, however, needs to be modiﬁed since the fact that F/N has only
periodic Abelian quotients does not imply that F/[N, N ] has the same property. To obtain an ordered group
H, therefore, a special action of G on an Abelian group A will be deﬁned throughout (9)-(14). Although
such an action looks rather complicated, still, it is then easy to show that H is totally ordered and H/H 
is periodic.

The consistency of deﬁning relations with (12)-(14) can be veriﬁed in a similar way.
    The split product A  G of an Abelian group A and a metabelian group G deﬁned via automorphisms
(9)-(14) will be a solvable group of length three. Let

                                          H = ci ai , bi,j ∈ A  G | i ∈ Z, j ∈ N < A  G.

We argue to show that H is orderable. To this end, we construct in H a series of normal subgroups satisfying
conditions of Kokorin’s theorem [9] (see also [4, Chap. II, Sec. 2, Thm. 3]):
    A group G is orderable if and only if there exists an infrainvariant series of subgroups Σ in G satisfying
the following condition: if A ≺ B is a jump in Σ then the quotient group B/A is N (A)/A-orderable.
    Put hi = ci ai and Hk = hi , bi,j | i ∈ Z, j ∈ N, i < kH , k ∈ Z. The subgroups Hk form a normal
series of subgroups, and     Hk = {1} and       Hk = H by construction. It remains to show that quotients

   Remark 3.3. In the previous example, all jumps in the series of normal convex subgroups of H are
Abelian by construction. In this connection, it is worth observing that H cannot have non-Abelian jumps
under any total ordering of H. This follows from a result by Medvedev [10, Thm. 2.2] (since H is metabelian-
by-periodic), or from a result of Glass and Medvedev [11, Prop. 1.3] (for H belongs to a variety AU, where
A is a variety of Abelian groups and U is a variety deﬁned by an unilateral identity [x, y 2 , y 2 ] = 1). We also
note that all orderable groups in U are nilpotent, but H/H  is not.
   Example 3.4. Now we use the group G given in Example 3.1 to construct a new group K as a split

group by an Abelian group). In fact, the derived length of this group equals four because the third derived
subgroup of K contains nontrivial elements. One such element will be needed below, and we so calculate it
now.

      Remark 3.5. The group K̄ in Example 3.4 was not ﬁnitely generated because the number of elements
                                                                                              ¯ h̄1 , b̄1,5  < K̄
b̄i,j was inﬁnite; but we used only one such element, namely, b̄1,5 . Thus, a subgroup K̄1 = d,
is 3-generated and has the same property as has K̄, i.e., K̄1 is solvable of length four with a sole proper
normal relatively convex subgroup. We are therefore faced up to an example of a ﬁnitely generated solvable
group of length four with only one proper normal relatively convex subgroup.
